goals: Set up null and alternative hypotheses
Explain Type I and Type II errors and statistical power
why: Hypothesis tests decide whether a new process, drug, price or website design really works, or whether the difference is just luck.
explain: Think of a **courtroom**. The **null hypothesis** (H₀) is "innocent": no effect, no difference. The **alternative** (H₁) is what you would like to show. You only reject H₀ if the evidence is strong.

The **p-value** is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme **if H₀ were true**. A small p (below the chosen α, often 0.05) means the data would be surprising under "no effect", so we reject H₀.
A p-value is **not** the probability that H₀ is true, and it says nothing about how large or important the effect is.

Two ways to be wrong: a **Type I error** (false positive: convicting the innocent, probability α) and a **Type II error** (false negative: letting the guilty go). **Power** = 1 − P(Type II) is the chance of detecting a real effect; it grows with sample size.

example.title: Is the coin fair?
steps: H₀: p(heads) = 0.5. Observed: 62 heads in 100 flips
z = (62 − 50) / 5 = 2.4 → two-sided p ≈ 0.016 (exact binomial test: p ≈ 0.021)
p < 0.05 → reject H₀ at the 5% level
example.result: The evidence suggests the coin is biased. A single test is still only one piece of evidence, so replicate before betting the company.

mistakes: "p = 0.03 means a 97% chance the effect is real" (wrong).
Treating p = 0.051 and p = 0.049 as completely different worlds.
Running many tests and reporting only the significant one (p-hacking).
Confusing statistical significance with business importance.
takeaways: H₀ = no effect; reject only on strong evidence
p-value = how surprising the data is if H₀ were true
Always report the effect size and a CI alongside p

practice.code:
from scipy.stats import binomtest
r = binomtest(62, 100, 0.5)
print(round(r.pvalue, 4), r.proportion_ci())
